nodes.name: Carbonization of Mo NPs
nodes.procedure: Commercial Mo nanoparticles (NPs) covered with amorphous carbon (Figure S1, Supporting information) were heated to 600°C under H₂ (5%)/Ar flow at a rate of 5°C min⁻¹. After being maintained at 600°C for 4 h and cooling to room temperature with the furnace, Mo NPs underwent a carbonization. All the prepared NPs showed exposed Mo₂C shells characterized by dense edge dislocations. The powder was referred to as the dislocation-rich Mo₂C.

nodes.source_text: Figure 1a illustrates the synthetic process of the dislocation-rich Mo₂C. Briefly, commercial Mo nanoparticles (NPs) covered with amorphous carbon were heated to 600°C under H₂ (5%)/Ar flow at a rate of 5°C min⁻¹. After being maintained at 600°C for 4 h and cooling to room temperature with the furnace, Mo NPs underwent a carbonization.

nodes.name: Dislocation annealing
nodes.procedure: For comparison, an annealing process at 800°C for 2 h (Figure S7, Supporting information) effectively eliminates dislocations from the dislocation-rich Mo₂C, as evidenced by HR-TEM images and XRD refinement (Figure S8 and S9, Supporting information). The obtained dislocation-free Mo₂C exhibits similar particle sizes, and crystal and electronic structures to that of the dislocation-rich Mo₂C.

nodes.name: Dislocation reduction annealing
nodes.procedure: A catalyst with a lower dislocation density was synthesized by annealing the dislocation-rich Mo₂C sample at a lower temperature (i.e., 700°C).
nodes.source_text: a catalyst with a lower dislocation density of 4.7 × 10¹⁰ mm⁻² (donated as dislocation-poor Mo₂C) was synthesized by annealing the dislocation-rich Mo₂C sample at a lower temperature (i.e., 700°C)

nodes.name: Compressed Mo2C preparation
nodes.procedure: A catalyst named 'compressed Mo₂C' using the same method as the dislocation-free Mo₂C but with a post-treatment to create solely compressive strains.

nodes.characterization_summary: SEM image reveals individual NPs with an average diameter of 47±1 nm.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The scanning electron microscope (SEM) image of the dislocation-rich Mo₂C (Figure 1b) reveals individual NPs with an average diameter of 47±1 nm (Figure S2, Supporting information).

nodes.characterization_summary: XRD confirms composition of Mo₂C (PDF #35-0787) and Mo (PDF #42-1120) with lattice strain from refinement corroborating dense dislocations in dislocation-rich Mo₂C.
nodes.evidence_snippet: X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis (Figure S3, Supporting information) confirms that the NPs are composed of Mo₂C (PDF #35-0787) and Mo (PDF #42-1120)... lattice strain obtained from XRD refinement also corroborates the presence of dense dislocations

nodes.characterization_summary: HAADF-STEM shows contrast difference between outer and inner areas of typical NPs suggesting carbonization of Mo on outermost shell.
nodes.evidence_snippet: High-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) images show a contrast difference between the outer and inner areas of typical NPs, suggesting the carbonization of Mo on the outermost shell

nodes.characterization_summary: EELS shows π* and σ* peaks of Mo₂C from NP surface.
nodes.evidence_snippet: which is further supported by the π* and σ* peaks of Mo₂C observed in electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) (Figure 1d, collected from Figure 1c)

nodes.characterization_summary: AES reveals characteristic negative peaks only for Mo₂C, indicating dense Mo₂C coating on all NPs.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Additionally, auger electron spectroscopy (AES) results (Figure 1e) of the catalysts reveal characteristic negative peaks only for Mo₂C

nodes.characterization_summary: HRTEM with FFT/IFFT reveals ultra-dense edge dislocations in Mo₂C areas; each dislocation induces compressive (0.22 nm, 6.7% strain vs theoretical d(002)=0.236 nm) and tensile (0.25 nm, 5.9% strain) regions.
nodes.evidence_snippet: High resolution transmission electron microscope (HR-TEM) images... Remarkably, ultra-dense edge dislocations can be observed in the Mo₂C areas... shortened (0.22 nm) representing a 6.7% compressive strain than the theoretical interplanar space d(002) = 0.236 nm... elongated lattice distances (0.25 nm) representing a 5.9% tensile strain

nodes.characterization_summary: GPA confirms coupled compressive-tensile strains present on every dislocation with strain intensity from -10% (compressive) to +10% (tensile).
nodes.evidence_snippet: The geometric phase analysis (GPA) results (Figure 1k, calculated from Figure 1j) further confirm that the coupled compressive-tensile strains are present on every dislocation

nodes.characterization_summary: In situ Raman shows Mo-H(tensile) at 1805 cm⁻¹ and Mo-H(compressive) at 1782 cm⁻¹ peaks on dislocation-rich Mo₂C at -0.03 V vs RHE.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In situ Raman spectroscopy was conducted... a broad peak of Mo-H was observed on the dislocation-rich Mo₂C at an extremely low overpotential (-0.03 V vs RHE, Figure 4b). The band could be resolved into two peaks, located at 1782 and 1805 cm⁻¹

nodes.characterization_summary: In situ ATR-FTIR confirms Mo-H(compressive) appears at -0.03 V vs RHE on dislocation-rich Mo₂C vs -0.18 V on compressed Mo₂C.
nodes.evidence_snippet: in situ, ATR-FTIR spectra for dislocation-free Mo₂C, compressed Mo₂C and dislocation-rich Mo₂C were analyzed individually... the Mo-H(compressive) in dislocation-rich Mo₂C appears at a lower potential (-0.03 V vs RHE)

nodes.characterization_summary: HRTEM confirms absence of dislocations in dislocation-free Mo₂C.
nodes.evidence_snippet: an annealing process at 800°C for 2 h effectively eliminates dislocations from the Mo₂C, as evidenced by HR-TEM images and XRD refinement (Figure S8 and S9, Supporting information)
